sections.title: Name and recognition
sections.text: This entry covers Gymnopilus junonius, also published under the synonym G. spectabilis. The cap is usually 5–15 cm across, sometimes larger; it begins convex with an inrolled margin, then spreads and may retain a low central bump. Its dry surface is ochre-yellow to orange or rusty brown, with radial fibres or small darker scales. The crowded gills are pale yellow to ochre, turning rusty brown as the spores mature; they are attached to the stem and may run slightly down it. The yellow to yellow-brown stem is fibrous, often swollen toward the base, and bears a more or less distinct ring that can become dusted with spores. The flesh is firm and yellow, the taste bitter, and the spore print rusty brown.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: This wood-decaying fungus grows in clusters on dead wood: stumps, logs, and sometimes the bases of living trees, mainly broadleaved trees in Europe. It has also been recorded on conifers. In temperate regions it appears mainly from late summer through autumn; timing varies with local climate.

sections.title: Similar species
sections.text: Orange colour and growth on wood are not enough to confirm this species. Honey fungus (Armillaria mellea) has a white spore print; Omphalotus illudens lacks a ring and has a pale spore print; other Gymnopilus species can look similar. Several characters and the habitat must be considered, and a wild collection should not be identified from an image alone.

sections.title: Toxicity and caution
sections.text: Do not eat it. The DGfM places G. junonius under psilocybin syndrome and notes gymnopilin. Scientific literature nevertheless reports conflicting results on detecting psilocybin in collections historically identified as G. spectabilis; that name has covered a taxonomic complex, so those results do not establish that every G. junonius specimen contains the compound. Poisonings and neurological effects have been reported, and the species is also described as very bitter. This entry cannot identify a collection or predict its effects.

traits: Cap usually 5–15 cm across, ochre-yellow to orange-brown, dry, fibrous or finely scaly
Crowded gills, pale yellow then rusty brown, attached to slightly decurrent; rusty spore print
Yellow to yellow-brown fibrous stem, often swollen toward the base and bearing a ring
Flesh firm and yellow, with a bitter taste
Clusters on stumps and dead wood, mainly broadleaved trees in Europe; late summer and autumn
safetyNote: Do not eat it: the DGfM places Gymnopilus junonius under psilocybin syndrome and notes gymnopilin. Psilocybin findings in collections identified under this name have been disputed, and the Gymnopilus junonius/spectabilis complex has unresolved taxonomic limits. The effects of a specimen therefore cannot be predicted from this entry. After ingestion, contact a poison centre or medical service.
